L01.title: What Is an API? Explained Simply
L01.summary: An API is a menu of requests one program may make to another. Your app sends a request, the server answers with structured data (usually JSON), and your app never sees how the server works inside.

L02.title: REST vs GraphQL: Which One Should You Use?
L02.summary: REST gives fixed-shape responses from many endpoints, which causes over-fetching and under-fetching. GraphQL has one endpoint and you ask for the exact shape you want. Pick by who is asking.

L03.title: gRPC vs WebSocket vs Webhook: When to Use Which
L03.summary: A webhook is the other service calling your URL, a WebSocket keeps one connection open both ways, and gRPC lets services call each other's functions with typed binary messages. Pick by who is talking.

L04.title: What Is MCP (Model Context Protocol)?
L04.summary: MCP replaces custom connectors between AI apps and tools with one shared standard: hosts, clients and servers that offer tools, resources and prompts. Build one server and every MCP app can use it.

L05.title: Bloom Filter: Check a Billion Usernames Without the Database
L05.summary: A Bloom filter is a row of bits. Any zero bit means 'definitely not present'; all ones means 'probably present'. Use it as a cheap gatekeeper in front of the database, never as the source of truth.

L06.title: How Websites Spot a Typo in Your Card Number (Luhn Check)
L06.summary: The Luhn algorithm uses the last digit as a check digit, so a mistyped number is rejected before any bank call. It catches typos only; it never proves a card is real.

L07.title: How OTP Expiry Actually Works
L07.summary: The server stores the code with a deadline (or a database TTL) and compares the time on use. Authenticator apps derive codes from a shared secret and the clock. Expiry is a stored deadline, not a running timer per code.

L08.title: Optimistic Locking: Two Users, One Seat, Same Millisecond
L08.summary: Both users read the seat at version 1. Each save says update only where the version is still 1, so the first wins and the second gets a conflict. Use it when clashes are rare, and take a real lock when they are not.

L09.title: How Websites Store Passwords (and Why Argon2id)
L09.summary: A good site never stores your password. It stores a salted, slow hash, so a leak doesn't hand attackers the originals. Use Argon2id.

L10.title: Why Is Kafka So Fast?
L10.summary: Kafka works with the disk and the OS instead of against them: append-only writes, batching, and skipping copies with the page cache and zero-copy sends.

T01.title: Why 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 in JavaScript
T01.summary: Computers store numbers in binary, where 0.1 repeats forever, so the stored values are only approximate. The tiny error shows up when you add, and the fix is to compare with a tolerance (epsilon) instead of ===.

T02.title: Cache Stampede: when one expired key kills your database
T02.summary: A popular cache entry expires, every request misses at the same moment, and all of them rebuild it from the database at once. Here is why it happens and how to stop it.

T03.title: Idempotency Keys: How Stripe Avoids Charging You Twice
T03.summary: Tap pay, the network times out, the app retries. An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry and return the first result instead of charging again.

T04.title: Why a SQL Index Makes Queries Instant
T04.summary: Without an index the database scans every row. An index is a sorted tree, like a book's index, so it jumps straight to the match. The catch: indexes cost write speed and space.

T05.title: JWT vs Session Cookie: What's the Real Difference?
T05.summary: Sessions keep your state on the server and give the browser an ID. A JWT carries signed proof in the token itself. The trade-off is revocation vs. statelessness.

T06.title: CAP Theorem Explained in 60 Seconds
T06.summary: When the network between two servers breaks, a distributed store must choose between consistency and availability. That is the real meaning of CAP.

T07.title: Why Your API Shouldn't Send Emails Directly (Use a Queue)
T07.summary: Sending the welcome email before responding makes users wait. A message queue lets the server answer immediately while a worker does the slow job in the background.

T08.title: The N+1 Query Problem: 101 Queries for One Page
T08.summary: One query for a list, then one more query per item inside a loop. Lazy loading hides it, and your database pays for it. Here is how to spot and fix it.

T09.title: CORS Error? Your Server Isn't Broken
T09.summary: CORS is a rule the browser enforces, not the server. Here is why your API works in Postman but fails in the browser, and what the server must send to allow another origin.

T10.title: Token Bucket: The Rate Limiter Behind Most APIs
T10.summary: A bucket holds a fixed number of tokens, refilled at a steady rate. Every request takes one. Empty bucket means the request is rejected, so one noisy client cannot slow everyone else.

T11.title: Docker vs Virtual Machine: Why Containers Start So Fast
T11.summary: A VM boots a whole operating system with its own kernel. A container is an isolated process sharing the host kernel, so there is nothing to boot.

T12.title: Exponential Backoff and Jitter: Stop Retry Storms
T12.summary: A thousand clients retry at once and knock the recovering server over again. Doubling the wait helps, and adding randomness (jitter) spreads the retries out.

T13.title: How 'Login with Google' Works (OAuth 2.0)
T13.summary: The app never sees your Google password. It redirects you to Google, gets an authorization code, and exchanges it for a token. Here is the flow, and why PKCE matters.

T14.title: Consistent Hashing: Add a Server Without Losing Your Cache
T14.summary: hash mod N remaps almost every key when N changes. Consistent hashing puts servers and keys on a ring so only nearby keys move.

T15.title: Why Is Redis So Fast? (It Uses One Thread)
T15.summary: Redis serves every request on a single thread, and it's still fast: data lives in memory, requests run one by one, and multiplexing watches many connections. The catch: one slow command like KEYS makes everyone wait.

T16.title: Deadlock: Two Transactions, Who Wins?
T16.summary: Each transaction holds the row the other needs, so both wait forever. PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one, and you can't predict which. Fix: lock rows in the same order, and retry.

T17.title: Spot the Bug in 3 Seconds: SQL Injection
T17.summary: Gluing user input into a SQL string lets ' OR 1=1 turn data into code. The fix is a parameterized query, not hand escaping, and ORMs are not safe if you concatenate there too.

T18.title: Git Doesn't Store Diffs. Here's What It Stores
T18.summary: Every commit is a snapshot, unchanged files are links to what Git already has, and everything is named by a hash of its contents. Change one byte and Git knows.

T19.title: ₹100 Left Your Account and Never Arrived. Where Is It?
T19.summary: A transfer is two steps. Crash between them without a transaction and the money vanishes. With BEGIN and COMMIT it's all or nothing, and committed data survives a crash.

T20.title: How Node.js Serves So Many Users on One Thread
T20.summary: Node never waits: network calls are non-blocking and slow file work goes to a worker pool, while the event loop moves on. The catch: one slow callback blocks everyone.

T21.title: Café Wi-Fi: Can a Stranger Read Your Password?
T21.summary: Over HTTP, yes. Over HTTPS, the TLS handshake checks the certificate and creates session keys, so captured packets look like nonsense. HTTPS protects the trip, not how the site stores it.

T22.title: Find 1 Key in a Million in 1 Step: Java HashMap
T22.summary: The hash code points straight to a bucket, so get and put are constant time. The map rebuilds at 75% full. The catch: keys with the same hash code pile into one bucket.

T23.title: You Press Enter. How Many Round Trips Before the Page?
T23.summary: DNS, then a TCP handshake (one round trip), then TLS 1.3 (one more): two round trips before the browser can even send GET, three with TLS 1.2. Distance makes every trip cost.

T24.title: Round Robin vs Least Connections: Which Server Gets It?
T24.summary: Round robin takes turns and ignores load. Least connections sends the request to the server with the fewest active connections. Neither helps with a dead server, so keep health checks on.

T25.title: Your App Crashes at 3 AM. Who Restarts It?
T25.summary: In Kubernetes, the kubelet restarts containers (restartPolicy Always) and liveness probes catch stuck apps. The catch: restarts back off 10s, 20s, 40s up to 5 minutes. That's CrashLoopBackOff.

T26.title: n² vs n log n at 1 Million Items: How Big Is the Gap?
T26.summary: A trillion steps versus twenty million, 50,000 times fewer. At an example billion steps per second, that's 17 minutes versus 20 ms. At 10 items the gap is tiny.

T27.title: Why Your Site Is Slow Far Away (and How a CDN Fixes It)
T27.summary: Every round trip crosses the distance. A CDN keeps copies of your content near users and cuts origin requests. The catch: copies go stale until the TTL expires or you purge.

T28.title: How Search Finds One Word in a Billion Documents
T28.summary: It doesn't read them at search time. An inverted index maps each word to the documents that contain it, built ahead of time. The price: every new document must be indexed first.
